en: The Seventy-sixth Fascicle of the Collected Explanations of the Treatise, Compiled by Shi Dunlun;
within the seven sections, this is the second, wherein the Bodhisattva Viśālamati inquires about mind, thought, and consciousness.
Within this, there is first a question and subsequently an answer.
The intent of the initial question is as follows:
"The Buddha speaks of a bodhisattva who is skilled in the secrets of mind, mentation, and consciousness."
"A Bodhisattva who is skillful regarding mind, mentation, and consciousness asks one question.
To what extent does the Tathāgata designate such a person as a Bodhisattva skilled in the secret of mind, mentation, and consciousness?"
This is the second question.
Of these two questions, the former concerns bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*),
while the latter concerns bodhisattvas on the stages.
The meanings of *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* possess both general and specific applications.
Regarding their specific designations as *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*: the *ālaya* is *citta*.
Because it is able to aggregate and give rise to the dharmas of form and mind within the cycle of birth and death in the three realms,
*manas* is so named.
Because it serves as the simultaneous basis for the six consciousnesses, giving rise to them, it is called the "mind."
The six consciousnesses are called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because they possess a strong power of discrimination with respect to the six objects.
All three are collectively termed "mind" (*citta*), "intellect" (*manas*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
This means that within each of the eight consciousnesses, there is a "mind" (citta) in the sense of being the collection and arising [of phenomena];
it is called "intellect" (manas) in the sense of being able to produce [mental activity]; and it is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) in the sense of discerning [objects]. Thus it is said.
In the response, first is the prose section,
second is the verse section;
the prose section is further divided into two parts.
First is the explanation, followed by the conclusion.
Within the former, there are two parts: first, praising his question and commanding him to listen while granting permission to speak;
second, the actual explanation.
The commentary consists of four parts:
first, explaining mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) with reference to the *ālayavijñāna*;
second, explaining the various names.
Third, it is established that the six consciousnesses depend upon the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
Fourth, it distinguishes whether Bodhisattvas possess skill or lack skill regarding the mind, thought, and consciousness.
Regarding the first point, the statement concerning "the maturation of all-seed consciousness from the beginning, throughout the cycle of birth and death in the six destinies," and so forth:
The seed-consciousness matures and draws forth the arising of *bhava* (existence).
Through the successive union of the *kalala* and so forth, the fetal parts develop and increase.
Based on these two types of appropriation (*upādāna*), it is clarified below that this *ālaya* possesses two modes of grasping.
The analysis of its maintenance according to the *dhātus* can be understood [as follows]:
although the ālayavijñāna takes the external vessel-world as its object, it does not grasp that world as an internal appropriated object (*upātta*), and therefore it is not mentioned here.
Next, the various names are analyzed.
Jingyun: This consciousness is also called ādāna;
this is translated as "grasping and maintaining."
That which grasps the material sense organs (*rūpindriya*) and the various seeds (*bīja*) is also called *ālaya*;
this is translated here as "the cherished store" (*ai-zang*).
It appropriates the body and,
furthermore, remains hidden within it, sharing its safety and peril;
for these reasons, it is also called "mind" (citta).
Why is this? Because by means of this consciousness, form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and so forth are accumulated and nourished; this has two meanings:
first, it can accumulate form and the other objects, and it can accumulate and nourish them.
Tài says: "Accumulation" (ji) is the meaning of the mind.
The desiring mind is able to accumulate and nourish the six sense objects, such as form and so forth.
The six sense organs and the six consciousnesses are common characteristics;
they are subsumed within the category of dharmas. However, only the six objects are explicitly mentioned here.
Bei said: From the six destinies up to the meaning of security and peril, there are three names in total used to explain the meaning of *vijñāna* (consciousness).
Furthermore, this serves as a prelude so that the meaning of *citta* (mind) may only then be explained below.
Briefly stated, the meaning is not understood.
The three knowledges establish the six consciousnesses:
first the principle, next the analogy, and finally the application.
Fazhong Tai says:
Although these three names are mentioned collectively in this prose section, the primary intent is to clarify *ādāna*.
Therefore, it specifically designates *ādāna* as the basis upon which the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) evolve.
In the subsequent verse, only the name *dhātu* (element) is recited; the intention lies herein.
The exposition of the meanings of "matter" (*rūpa*) and "mind" (*citta*) is hereby complete.
To distinguish the meaning,
the sense of the basis is used to manifest the general meaning of the arising of consciousness.
Within this context, "consciousness exists" up to "the conceptualizing mental consciousness evolves."
Tài says: Because there is an eye-faculty that is of the same class as visual consciousness,
it is said to be "the eye and visible forms," and so forth.
There is the ādāna-vijñāna which is capable of receiving [seeds];
next, it is called "vijñāna.
In the analogy, two metaphors are briefly cited.
What is the distinction?
An ancient master said:
"The surface of a mirror is a metaphor for the gate of the suchness of the mind."
The metaphor of the water waves illustrates the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind.
Now, Master Xuanzang says that the explanations of these two metaphors by the various masters of the West are identical.
However, because one desires to clarify the fundamental meaning, two similes are required.
The application of the similes follows the text.
Fourth, there is the discernment of whether a bodhisattva possesses skill or lack thereof regarding mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammatthitiñāṇa*):
if one explains the knowledge of the stability of phenomena according to the *Cūḷaniddesa*,
it is the knowledge that the fruits— superior, middling, and inferior— of the three realms abide within their causes.

Now, based on the Mahāyāna or based on the scriptural teachings, because one understands the meaning of mind (*citta*), mentation (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dharmasthitijñāna*).
Alternatively, based on the conventional principle of cause and effect, knowing the names of mind, mentation, and consciousness is called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena."
Although there are two interpretations that both rely on conventional knowledge (*yathāvadbhāva-jñāna*) to understand mind, mentation,
and consciousness as being situated in the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), the Tathāgatas do not hear this being designated as "skillfulness."
The following clarifies that bodhisattvas on the stages are established as being skillful.
If bodhisattvas do not, within themselves individually, perceive the *ādāna* (appropriating consciousness) as it truly is, they do not perceive its function.
"Not seeing the ādānavijñāna" means not seeing its essence;
the same applies to the subsequent phrases.
Thus, at the time of realizing *tathatā*, not seeing any phenomena is what is called a "skillful bodhisattva of the ultimate truth."
The Tathāgata established the fetters as described in the text.
Among these, the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) does not arise based on [scriptural] teaching;
it is capable of manifesting whether [the teaching] is explained or not.
Now, because one wishes to distinguish [the afflictions] that arise simultaneously (*sahaja*),
the term "conceptual" (*vikalpa*) is employed.
The remaining phrases are as usual.
The master Asaṅga cites this verse to explain the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
while Vasubandhu cites the prose commentary to explain the meaning of this verse;
these details are fully set forth therein.
From this point on begins the third major section, which elucidates the Bodhisattva’s inquiry into the meaning of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Therefore, it says: "skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena.
As before, there are two initial questions.
In the response, there is first the prose (gadya) and subsequently the verse (śloka).
The prose section has two parts:
first, the explanation, and second, the conclusion.
In the first part, there is first the praise, the inquiry, and the consent to speak;
second, the actual explanation.
Within the explanation, there are six successive sections.
First, it is said that there are three characteristics of all phenomena:
first, the imagined; second, the dependent; and third, the perfected.
The statement from "the imagined nature" up to "in order to give rise to conventional expression" clarifies the intent behind such discourse.
Sentient beings, out of ignorance, grasp at names as being real; this is the *parikalpita* (imagined nature).
That which is called "dependent" refers to defiled phenomena that arise.
The *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature) is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
The assembly of bodhisattvas, taking diligence as their cause, is able to attain thorough penetration;
they gradually realize and perceive this within the stages until it reaches fulfillment at the stage of Buddhahood.
The first explanation is concluded.
Second, once again, it is elucidated by means of the analogy of visual impairment (*timira*).
Zhongjing says:
Regarding the statement, "The grasping [at objects] by those afflicted with the defect of cataracts is likewise," it is asked:
Are cataracts conditioned phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna*)?
How is it that this serves as an analogy for the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)?
The explanation states:
it does not take up the visual impairment (*timira*).
This clarifies that the false perception of floating hairs due to visual impairment serves as an analogy for the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
hence, it speaks of "the affliction of visual impairment.
To say that "just as a person with visual impairment sees floating hairs and so forth, so too is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)" means:
The hair-tufts and so forth are precisely the parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature).
One does not intend to take these as an analogy for the paratantra-svabhāva (dependent nature);
rather, the intent is to clarify that because of this grasping at hair-tufts, the consciousness is perfumed to form seeds, which give rise to the subsequent paratantra.
Just as a person with clear vision perceives the fundamental nature of phenomena,
so too does fundamental wisdom realize the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Tái said:
Those with the affliction of visual impairment (timira) grasp [the appearance] as being fixed and real; the term "hair, fur, and so forth" refers generally to such afflictions.
This serves as a metaphor for phenomena that are grasped through pervasive conceptual construction (parikalpita-svabhāva) as having a fixed existence.
If the visual consciousness of one with impaired vision transforms [itself] into hair, fur, and so forth...
That which arises from causes and conditions has no fixed nature; this is analogous to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
By this, it is demonstrated that even one who perceives a second moon sees a semblance of a moon manifested by a deranged visual consciousness.
This is a phenomenon of dependent origination that can produce visual consciousness; however,
according to the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the second moon lacks any intrinsic nature because it is grasped as having a fixed existence.
It cannot produce consciousness;
therefore, it is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, it is explained that this treatise refutes those false views according to the tenets of the Hīnayāna school.
The Hīnayāna school asserts that the second moon lacks substantial reality;
therefore, visual consciousness cannot take it as its object. Bei states:
The metaphor of the affliction of visual impairment and dizziness represents the two types of grasping— toward persons and phenomena—
and the objects of pervasive conceptualization, such as floating hairs, eyelashes, and so forth;
the phrase "and so forth" includes the second moon and other such illusions.
This is precisely the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Therefore, the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
"The form that is the object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) refers to reflected form (*pratibimba-rūpa*)."
Question:
If it is admitted that dependent form exists, for what reason is it also considered to be the object of parikalpita (imagined)? Answer:
Because it necessarily arises from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*),
it is called "pervasive conceptualization" according to its object; in reality, however,
it depends upon the dependent nature (*paratantra*).
It is like seeing a face by relying on a mirror;
the face itself has four aspects: first, the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
Second, the face manifested by the visual consciousness;
third, the face arising from the mental consciousness that takes the same object;
fourth, the face manifested as an object by the independent mental consciousness.
Among these four aspects, the first is the actual object itself.
The second and third resemble the actual object and are therefore called "dependent origination" (*paratantra*).
The final one appears within the mirror apart from the location of the actual object.
It is called "universal imagination" (parikalpita) simply because it arises from universal imagination;
however, speaking in terms of ultimate reality, there are two aspects within it:
first, the dependent aspect of the objective part (nimitta-bhāga).
Second is the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). A certain master explains:
within a single visual consciousness, there are two objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*).
That is to say, [the object consists of] both the actual moon and the second moon;
this explanation is incorrect,
because it cannot be designated as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Because the five consciousnesses cannot be deceived.
Now, this shall be explained.
Visual consciousness arises based on the actual moon;
it is merely within the mind of the mental consciousness that the interpretation of two moons occurs.
In the third section, first the analogy of the crystal is presented, followed by its application to the Dharma.
Regarding the term *sphatika* mentioned previously:
the Tripiṭaka Master stated that there is no corresponding name here [in Chinese] that can be translated.
It resembles crystal or white pearls;
it has no fixed color and combines with the four colors.
It appears as images of four colors that delude sentient beings;
with a perverted mind, they grasp them as real,
speaking of them as "images of the indranīla and mahānīla maṇi jewels."
In Sanskrit it is called Indra;
here it is translated as Śakra.
This is the blue maṇi jewel of Śakra.
In the western region there is a blue jewel;
its color resembles the blue jewel of Śakra,
and thus it is named accordingly.
This is the residual blue color within the blue.
In Sanskrit it is called mahānīla, which means "blue";
it is specifically a deep, dark blue.
*Maṇi* is a Sanskrit term;
it is the general name for a jewel.
*Māṇikya* is... [the specific name for a ruby].
Jingyun: There is no name here that can be translated.
Taiyun said:
This is the "Killing Color" jewel of this region;
its color is green. Jing said:
This is called musāragalva.
How much more so when it is said that within the Dharma, the correspondence of the coloring upon that pure crystal—even extending to its habitual tendencies—is likewise so.
The meaning is that the "grasping subject" and the "grasped object" are the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from former lives.

To say that "the grasping for the characteristics of the grasped object, which arises based on the appearance of false attachments such as indranīla or mahānīla upon a pure crystal, is likewise [the case here]" means that it is exactly so.
This [first phrase] combines with the grasper;
this [second phrase] brings forth that which is grasped by the grasper.
Therefore, these two phrases together constitute the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Regarding the statement, "One should know that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is likewise like that pure crystal gem," the crystal gem itself corresponds to the dependent nature.
It should be understood that the statement "just as that [crystal] is pure, even so is the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva)" is to be known.
Question:
It can be understood that the crystal gem serves as an analogy for the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
When a crystal gem is combined with four colors, four colored images arise; this is analogous to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
When one clings to the dependent and the perfected natures (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as being real, there is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
It can also be understood that the absence of intrinsic nature in objects grasped through pervasive conceptualization reveals the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Why, then,
does the treatise not include here the factors of the causes and conditions for the images of the four types of form?
The commentary explains:
The crystal gem (*sphaṭika*) serves as an analogy for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the ālayavijñāna;
the four-colored images appear because of the crystal.
For example, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the six consciousnesses is the reflection of the objective aspect of the ālayavijñāna,
and it is also its support (*āśraya*).
If one analyzes this in detail:
The dharma and the analogy are not identical;
therefore, it is omitted here.
Regarding the fourth point, it is stated that because one clings to names and signs as being fixedly associated, the grasped signs become cognizable through those conditions.
Because the seeds perfumed by the grasping of the thoroughly imagined nature can give rise to the subsequently arising dependent nature,
it is said that the dependent nature can be understood as having the grasped object as its condition;
thus, the thoroughly imagined characteristic serves as the condition.
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) can be understood;
according to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, it itself possesses five aspects.
The first is the aspect of the grasped (*grāhya-lakṣaṇa*).
Second is the characteristic of the grasper;
third is the characteristic of attachment to the connection between name and characteristic;
fourth is the characteristic of clinging.
Regarding the five aspects of non-attachment:
the first two pertain to all three natures,
while the third is precisely the nature of pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).
The fourth is the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*);
the fifth is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).
Now, the Master of the Treatise provides the following explanation.
By means of the third characteristic, the apprehended characteristic and so forth can be understood;
this fifth section further clarifies the benefits of the three natures.
"To understand the perfected nature is to understand all that is pure."
This is because the purified dependent nature belongs to the perfected nature.
The sixth section further clarifies the benefits of abandonment and realization:
if one can thoroughly understand the signlessness of the dependent nature, [the benefits follow].
"It is able to sever defilement and realize purity.
Thus, from the phrase "the root of virtue" (*guṇamūla*) onwards, the three subsequent sections are cited to conclude the answers to the two preceding questions.
The first three successive sections have been omitted for brevity.
The final two lines of the two verses are difficult to understand.
The Tripitaka Master explains them as follows:
Those who are indolent do not cultivate the foundation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Abiding in the Dharma is concentration;
within the realm of movement lies distraction (*vikṣepa*).
There is no one to be pitied who has undergone ruin or destruction due to indolence.
That which is the unsurpassed state of abiding is called "non-existence";
that which is the surpassable state of movement is called "existence."
Because they lack stability and possess distraction,
they lose the True Dharma within their bodies;
this is called "ruination."
Therefore, he is to be pitied. Tai said:
"Abiding in dharmas is fixedness."
The nature of movement is disorder.
There are two ways in which it is lost and destroyed:
first, because it is a phenomenon that does not abide, it is lost and destroyed.
Secondly, because they possess the nature of instability, they undergo ruin;
at the time of such ruin, it is always due to indolence that this occurs.
For this reason, they are to be pitied.
Jingyun: The nature of reality is neither born nor extinguished;
therefore, it is called the "abiding dharma."
The imagined nature and the dependent nature undergo arising and ceasing;
therefore, they are called "moving phenomena.
One who is indolent regarding these moving phenomena loses what is non-existent and destroys what exists.
Therefore, it is said that there is no loss or destruction.
"Non-existence" refers to the principle of true reality, which is emptiness;
"existence" refers to the falsely existent phenomena of the dependent and the imagined natures.
This person has lost and destroyed the principle of the three natures;
therefore, they are to be pitied. Furthermore, there is another interpretation.
This is a protracted statement, meaning that one who dwells in indolence within the states of movement and flux is pitiable as they lack any capacity for non-destruction.
This concludes the fourth major section: the inquiry by the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata regarding the meaning of the three natures.
The text contains four sections.
The first consists of questions and answers that clarify the meaning of the three natures (trisvabhāva).
The second is the acceptance of the teaching and the expression of praise.
The third [section] distinguishes the superiority and inferiority of the teachings and the merit of upholding the sūtra;
the fourth [section] requests the establishment of the sūtra’s title and describes how the assembly gains benefit at that time.
Within the former [section], there are two parts.
First, the Bodhisattva poses the question;
second, the Buddha provides the answer.
Within the former, this is the intent of the inquiry.

In various sūtras, the Blessed One has taught the arising and ceasing, the defilement and purification, the knowing, abandoning, realizing, and cultivating of the manifold phenomena such as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Later, he further taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, without arising or ceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature nirvāṇa.
Do these two preceding explanations not contradict each other?
From here on, the author will respond.
First, he praises the question as excellent, commands attention, and grants permission to speak.
Thereafter follows the formal response.
Within the response, there is first the prose and subsequently the verse restatement.
The prose section consists of five successive segments.
First, understanding that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and are without arising or ceasing;
second, understanding the establishment of the three kinds of non-nature as causes and conditions;
third, understanding the teaching of the three non-natures according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Fourth, the intention of the One Vehicle as explained according to the secret [teachings].
Fifth, clarifying that there are four types of sentient beings who possess either understanding or lack thereof regarding the Buddha’s secret teachings.
Within the first [of these two], there are two [subdivisions].
First, the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is analyzed;
subsequently, the absence of arising and ceasing and so forth are analyzed.

Within the former, the statement "I have spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature based on the three kinds of absence of intrinsic nature" is a general presentation of the underlying intent of the teaching.
This refers to the enumeration of the three natures (trisvabhāva) following the discussion on the lack of intrinsic nature in characteristics (lakṣaṇaniḥsvabhāvatā),
which is explained through a series of questions and answers. Within this section, first the meaning is established by way of doctrine (dharmadeśanā), followed by illustrative analogies (dṛṣṭānta).
In the explanation of the Dharma,
the thoroughly imagined nature is the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics.
The dependent nature can be understood as possessing both [types of] selflessness:
namely, the selflessness of arising and the selflessness of the ultimate.
T'ai says: Because the dependent nature lacks the true suchness of ultimate reality,
it is therefore called the "ultimate lack of intrinsic nature."
I have prepared two interpretations.
The first states that because the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) does not exist within the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva),
it is called "the absence of nature in the ultimate sense" (paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā).
This refers to the meaning of mutual non-existence.
One interpretation states that if one explains the dependent nature (*paratantra*) by means of ultimate reasoning (*paramārtha-yukti*),
it exists only as a provisional existence based on conditions.
It does not possess a real intrinsic nature;
therefore, it is said to be "without nature in the ultimate sense.
This does not mean that because the other-dependent nature lacks the meaning of the perfected nature, it is called "without intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense."
Although the latter explanation is offered,
it does not equal the former.

As for the statement that "the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) exists solely by virtue of the lack of intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense (paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā), because the selflessness of all phenomena is called the ultimate sense," and so forth:
Jingyun said:
"One should not take non-self to be the perfected reality (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
The perfected reality is, in fact, True Suchness (tathatā)."
However, because one enters by way of the door of selflessness,
it is said from the perspective of that entry-door that selflessness is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Suchness (*tathatā*) is the essence of the ultimate truth of all phenomena, as it is manifested through the door of signlessness (*animitta*).
Therefore, it is said that the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is called "the absence of intrinsic nature" (niḥsvabhāva). Beiyun states:
"To distinguish the essence of suchness (tathatā), the nature of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) is also called the ultimate truth."
Because it is manifested by the various kinds of non-nature previously distinguished,
it is called "the nature of being without self-nature.
The analogies can be understood accordingly.
"Good son" and below concludes the answer to the preceding question. Next,
it distinguishes [the state of] being without arising or ceasing, and so forth.
First, it is explained in terms of the thoroughly imagined nature;
second, it is explained in terms of the perfected nature.
Regarding the former:
Jingtai and others said:
"Because the pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita) has no essence whatsoever, it has no arising;
if there is no nature, then there is no cessation."
Because it is without arising or ceasing, it is primordially quiescent;
the meaning of this quiescence is similar to *nirvāṇa*, and thus it is called *nirvāṇa*.
It is not the *nirvāṇa* of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Bei said: "The previous virtuous masters and others interpreted this as intending to distinguish the counteractive measure against pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita) and true nirvana."
Therefore, it is said that "intrinsic nature is nirvāṇa.
To explain this now:
this refers to the nirvāṇa of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), not to true nirvāṇa.
The following section establishes that the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is without arising or ceasing.
Whereas the preceding [section] maintained that there is no arising or ceasing because the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) lacks intrinsic existence,
this [section] maintains that there is no arising or ceasing because the perfected nature is eternal by its very essence.
Because that which arises and ceases through the illusory conditions of others cannot be established as having arising and ceasing when examined,
this distinction is made according to the categories of the three natures (trisvabhāva).
Regarding the previous analysis of the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) based on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*),
the principle is that the absence of characteristics (*animitta*) in the purely imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) alone exhausts the meaning of the absence of nature;
this is as stated in the subsequent passage below.
Thereafter, speaking further in terms of the points of delusion and attachment,
it is said that "subsequently, the dependent nature is established as being without self-nature,
and the ultimate nature is without self-nature."

The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*). Second, the reasons for establishing the three types of lack of intrinsic nature are clarified. Regarding the statement, "It is not because [I have established] the three types of lack of intrinsic nature within the realm of sentient beings," and so forth: it means that I have not established these three types of lack of intrinsic nature based on the perspective of the realm of sentient beings. Rather, I have established them based on the perspective of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This is because the Dharma-realm is the basis for both the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Since the Dharma-realm is itself devoid of intrinsic nature, it is therefore called the "ultimate lack of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, because the Dharma-realm is the basis for the imagined nature, it is therefore called the "lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*). Because the Dharma-realm is the basis for the dependent nature, it is therefore called the "lack of intrinsic nature in terms of arising" (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*). Jingyun: The three natures (*trisvabhāva*) in principle are all the naturelessness of the imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
However, this is merely for the purpose of distinguishing the locus of the conceptual construction of the imagined nature.
The lack of nature in arising and the lack of nature in the ultimate sense are distinguished in relation to the dependent and the thoroughly established natures;
alternatively, the lack of nature in arising and the lack of nature in the ultimate sense are distinguished in relation to the basis of what is imagined.
This also exhaustively encompasses the lack of intrinsic nature;
if one were to say "the lack of intrinsic nature of the imagined characteristic," this would likewise exhaustively encompass the absence of nature.

If one distinguishes the lack of intrinsic nature in arising and the lack of intrinsic nature in the ultimate truth by way of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*),
these also exhaustively encompass all aspects of the lack of intrinsic nature;
thus, they are counted as one and two combined.
Thus, there are three kinds of naturelessness.
Therefore, this text states: "It is not because I observe the three natures separately that I establish the three kinds of naturelessness;

rather, it is because sentient beings adhere to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) according to verbal designations that I establish the three kinds of naturelessness."
Tài said: "If one contemplates upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature) that it lacks the nature superimposed by the *parikalpita* (the imagined nature),
this is precisely the *parikalpita-niḥsvabhāvatā* (the absence of nature in the imagined)."
This is also the nature of non-arising of the dependent;
likewise, when one observes that even upon the perfected nature there is no imagined nature,
this is the signlessness of the imagined nature.
This is also the nature of the non-substantiality of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
According to this text, one observes that within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature, there is no imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
therefore, among the three natures, the imagined nature lacks intrinsic substance.
Therefore, it is said to be "without nature.
Because the dependent and the perfected natures lack the essence of the imagined nature,
they are said to be without nature.
The phrase "or by means of verbal expression, one cognizes accordingly" refers to sentient beings who,
through their conceptualization of names and words,
give rise to pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpa*).
Regarding the phrase "due to the latent tendencies of verbal expression":
this refers to infants, cattle, sheep, and other sentient beings who do not understand linguistic conventions;
although they do not understand such conventions, they nevertheless give rise to conceptual discrimination.
Nevertheless, due to the power of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the seeds of conventional expression,
one makes general conceptual estimations; thus,
in accordance with the capacities of those to be trained, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are taught through three modes of contemplation.
Within this, first the three natures are distinguished with reference to the forty stages of mind;
next, they are distinguished with reference to the four stages of the roots of goodness;
and finally, they are distinguished with reference to the stages beyond the world (bhūmi).

Fourth, regarding the explanation of the intention behind the One Vehicle from a secret perspective:

For this reason, the Buddha, for the sake of the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have first turned toward the Mahāyāna, refuted their attachment to existence.
The intentional (saṃdhāya) general teaching that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), without arising or ceasing, and so forth,

Question: If it is said that this Esoteric Teaching explains the three natures of non-existence (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), does the intent of the Prajñāpāramitā teachings also explain the nature of the reality of non-existence (*tathatā-niḥsvabhāvatā*)?
Answer: Yes.
The teaching explicitly states only that "all things are non-existent" without making further distinctions; however,
if one grasps the underlying intent of the teaching,
it universally reveals the principle of the three natures of non-nature.
Therefore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other [sūtras] reveal their underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) by correctly elucidating the three kinds of lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

"The teaching that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, are without arising or cessation, are primordially quiescent, and are by nature in nirvāṇa, is taught with the intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) of the lack of intrinsic nature."
Thus we know that this merely reveals the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Within this sutra, there are four types of persons explained below in detail.

"Up to this point, it is known only by those of subtle, thorough, and discerning wisdom;

The third type refers to those sentient beings who, having not yet accumulated superior provisions and lacking an upright nature,
remain within dogmatic adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), even though they possess the capacity for discernment regarding what to adopt and what to reject.
If they hear such a teaching as this,
they will lack the power to understand my profound speech of intentional meaning;
though they may give rise to faith and understanding, they will cling to the literal words.
It means that all phenomena are definitively without intrinsic nature, neither arising nor ceasing.

This is like the scholars of the Three Treatises who, being attached to the view of emptiness,

Regarding those who conceive the notion of "meaning" within what is not the meaning:
they simultaneously discard the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) while failing to realize that the remaining two natures are not empty;
thus, they conceive the notion of "emptiness" regarding the non-empty meaning of those remaining two natures.
Even though their merit increases because they have developed faith in the teachings,
their wisdom declines because they give rise to attachment toward what is not the true meaning.

All wise persons believe that when the Buddha taught that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing and so forth, these were spoken with a specific hidden intent.

Regarding the phrase "the subtle, inconceivable, untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu), within which liberation is equal and without distinction":

The noble ones of the three vehicles equally awaken to this principle;
therefore, it is said that regarding liberation therein, there is no distinction.
As for "all meanings accomplished and free from delusion and suffering":
Because one realizes the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it is called "the accomplishment of all purposes" (*sarvārthasiddhi*).

and it is blissful because it is free from suffering.
The two names "Constant" (*nitya*) and "Blissful" (*sukha*) refer to two different explanations.
