Third, regarding the immeasurable light of the non-differentiated characteristics of the ten directions: it is the thorough understanding [of them].
This is the fruit of effortless cultivation (*anābhoga-bhāvanā*).
By virtue of having correctly realized the post-meditative wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that transcends meditative absorption,
one illuminates the non-differentiated characteristics of the worlds of the ten directions, just as before.
It is called the "Light of Dharma.
Fourth, as for the aspect of non-conceptualization in which the pure portion corresponding to the fulfillment of what is to be done is constantly present before one:
this is the fruit of intense cultivation.
The fruit of Buddhahood in the future is called the "fulfillment-corresponding pure portion.
Because this intense cultivation is for the purpose of inducing that fruit,
non-conceptual signs constantly manifest before one.
Fifth, regarding "gathering the progressively superior and more excellent causes in order to bring the dharmakāya to full completion":
this refers to the fruit of cultivation characterized by non-contentment,
which is perfected at the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
Because the names of the Buddhas have been fulfilled,
the cause that brings about this result is called "supremely sublime."
Because they are summoned and accumulated by each preceding cause,
they are called the "appropriation of subsequent causes that are increasingly superior and sublime.
The fourth [section] clarifies thorough penetration.

Furthermore, that which is called "thorough penetration" from the first stage, the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and is called "attainment" from the third stage, the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*),
refers to the śamatha and vipaśyanā cultivated by taking the universal dharma as its object.
Because one has realized the exhaustion of principles,
it is said that from the first bhūmi onward, one is called "thoroughly penetrating" (*prativedha*).
This is stated in terms of characteristics, as one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the third bhūmi.
It is said that from the third bhūmi onward, one is said to have "attained" [the realization].

Regarding the statement "a bodhisattva at the stage of initial practice should not be indolent," this means that even bodhisattvas prior to the bhūmis study the contemplation of true suchness (*tathatā*), the contemplation of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), among other things.
Although it may not yet be possible to sigh with joy, one should not become lax or negligent; rather, one should diligently cultivate contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and tranquility (*śamatha*).
This is the second sequential explanation of the thirteenth stage-gate.
Jingchu explains *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Regarding the modes of activity associated with the characteristics of the phenomena that are apprehended as they are, there are coarse and subtle aspects, which constitute the former two types [of vitarka and vicāra]. If,
with respect to those very same characteristics of all phenomena, there is no mental engagement (*manasikāra*), nor reception, nor investigation, this is called "without vitarka and without vicāra."
This training in the contemplation of suchness, which is non-conceptual contemplation,
is called "without vitarka and vicāra.
These three are all situated prior to the stages (bhūmi).
The practice is divided into three parts;
it is not distinguished according to stages such as the desire realm or the first dhyāna.
In the second explanation, the four investigations constitute the first phrase.
The fourth, thorough knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*), constitutes the second phrase;
non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*) constitutes the third.
These are also not distinguished according to the stages (*bhūmi*).
However, regarding the three [categories] according to practice (*caryā*), Tai says:
"The preceding 'furthermore' (*punar-aparam*) distinguishes them based on practice."
Therefore, it pervades the three realms.
The subsequent sequential analysis, which distinguishes according to the stages (*bhūmi*),
is identical in meaning to that found in the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
The eleventh is the gate of the three characteristics.
Jing says: Regarding the statement from "if the mind is agitated" up to "this is called the characteristic of cessation":
If the mind becomes agitated or arises with respect to an object that causes agitation,
one should attend to and contemplate phenomena that are loathsome,
as well as attend to and contemplate the continuity of the loathsome mind itself.
This is called the characteristic of tranquility (*śamatha*).

Regarding the statement "if the mind sinks... this is called the characteristic of uplifting (*pragraha*)," it refers to when the mind has sunk, or when it is facing an object that causes sinking, or when there is fear that the mind will sink.
One attends to and contemplates phenomena that are inspiring,
or one takes as an object the continuity of that very mind within its own kind;
this is called the sign of uplifting.

Regarding the statement, "If, in the path of exclusive calm abiding (*śamatha*), this is called the characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā-nimitta*)," this refers to the fact that in the paths of exclusive calm abiding, exclusive insight (*vipaśyanā*), and their union,
both secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and so forth are obstacles to equanimity.
Now, being free from those hindrances,
there is effortless mental attention (*anābhoga-manasikāra*) and all forms of mental attention occurring within the spontaneous engagement of the mind.
This is called the mark of equanimity (*upekṣā-nimitta*).
Tái says: "Concentration is called the mark of cessation (*śamatha-nimitta*)."
Because one relies on that which has previously ceased and on the immediate [condition],
and because there is no aspect of the object to be observed that is not conducive to joy, one attains the cessation of restlessness.
This is the twelfth gate, the knowledge of the meaning of phenomena (*dharmārtha*).
First the question is posed, then the answer follows.
Within the answer, first the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is distinguished,
followed by the knowledge of meaning (*arthajñāna*).
Master Jingyun states: "Names express their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, the aforementioned treatise speaks of 'the superimposition of self-nature' (*svabhāva-adhyāropa*)."
A phrase (*pada*) expresses the distinct meanings of various phenomena, such as impermanence and so forth.
Therefore, the aforementioned treatise states: "A phrase is a further verbal expression that differentiates.
A syllable (*vyañjana*) is able to combine names (*nāman*) and phrases.
It is called the basis for names;
that is to say, by means of attention directed toward individual objects,
the mind of naming arises.
This means that by means of the attention directed toward the synthesized object,
one gives rise to the mind of the opening statement and the two subsequent types of minds that initiate the teaching of the Dharma.
The name "wén" (pattern/letter) refers to the "fǎ" (dharma). Tái says:
it refers to the meanings of defilement and purity that are expressed.
Because it relies upon names and phrases, it is established as that which expresses meaning;
therefore, it is called "the basis for establishment.
"Phrases" (vyañjana) refers to conventional speech.
Now, using conventional characters to manifest those scriptural characters,
one understands the meaning through ten aspects, beginning with the characters that serve as the basis for both names and phrases.
Second, knowing five kinds;
third, knowing four kinds;
fourth, knowing three kinds.
Regarding the ten kinds of knowledge:
first is the knowledge of the nature of exhaustiveness (*yāvadbhāvikatā*),
which is the limit of the various categories of defiled and purified phenomena.
Second is knowing the nature of things as they are (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*),
which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
Below, seven kinds of suchness are distinguished.
The Master Ki and others say that the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* also clarifies these seven.
An older scholar says:

Regarding the seven kinds of true suchness (*tathatā*) in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, they are designated as "suffering" or the "truth of suffering" and so forth according to their respective designations (*vyañjana*).
Now, to explain the intent of this treatise: it is because the truths of suffering and the rest are themselves termed "true suchness."
The name "True Suchness" (tathatā) does not itself constitute the essence of True Suchness.
According to this treatise, all things are indeed True Suchness;
however, when distinguished by way of their designations, there are seven kinds.
There is an interpretation:
the principle of the systematic establishment of the sevenfold dharma is subsumed under the principle of logic;
this is precisely what is called *tathatā* (suchness).
This further consists of seven types.
First, regarding the nature of circulation (*pravṛtti-svabhāva*), which refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have no priority or posteriority:
the circulation of all conditioned phenomena is without beginning and without end.
Therefore, it is said that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) lack the nature of priority or posteriority.
To discern this principle is precisely what is called "suchness" (tathatā).
This is the second aspect of suchness.
The absence of self in both persons and phenomena is their characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The true suchness (*tathatā*) that constitutes the essence of this characteristic is called the "true suchness of characteristics.
Therefore, it is stated below: "Eighth, because of thoroughly understanding the meaning of the true suchness of characteristics."
There are persons who lack the characteristics of selflessness and so forth;
these are countered by ultimate emptiness and the like.
Third, the thorough discernment of suchness, namely that all conditioned phenomena are of the nature of consciousness alone.
The essence of consciousness is discernment;
this discerning consciousness is the essential characteristic of all phenomena,
and is thus termed the "suchness of discernment."
Fourth, the suchness of establishment refers to the fact that the truth of suffering is truly suffering and cannot be made into pleasure; this is called suchness.
The same applies to the other three truths.
All four truths are established [doctrines].
Suffering (duḥkha) is the very first to receive the designation "established," while the remaining three can be understood by their respective specific names that are subsequently applied.
The following section distinguishes between the universal and the specific. Among these seven, the three— namely, the flow, the establishment, and the wrong practice—
are common to all sentient beings.
The suchness of the two kinds of selflessness;
the suchness of consciousness-only; and the equal existence of all phenomena.
Because it penetrates all phenomena,
the suchness of purity is equal across the three vehicles.
Because the three vehicles eliminate afflictions and equally realize cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This cessation through deliberation and true thusness (*tathatā*) are common to all three vehicles by virtue of the true thusness of correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti-tathatā*).
The equality of śamatha and vipaśyanā;
this demonstrates four kinds of equality.
Regarding the fifth point, the meaning of establishment: it refers to the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) within which all realms of sentient beings and so forth can be established.
The formation of the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) that receives sentient beings is called "establishment" (vyavasthāna).
That is, the realm of sentient beings is what is established;
here, the intended meaning refers to the establishment of the vessel-world itself.
Therefore, the text says: "That is to say, one village field, or a hundred village fields, and so forth.

The remaining passages may be understood accordingly. Among the five meanings, that which is the thorough knowledge of the object (*vastu*) is the knowledge of the essence (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
The meaning of "thoroughly knowing" (*parijñā*) is the meaning of knowing distinctions.
"Condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to the four conditions.
"Time" (*adhvan*) refers to the three times.
Regarding the statement "the cause of thorough knowledge," it should be understood as that which is able to grasp the aforementioned two factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*),
and so forth. T'ai says:
The four foundations of mindfulness constitute one [category].
The four right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are collectively treated as one.
These two are called "two" because they are capable of attaining bodhi.
Another interpretation is that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are said to be "two" because they take the preceding two objects as their conditions. Jing says:
Since it was previously stated that there is the unsurpassed bodhi and the bodhi of the two vehicles,
it is said here that these are "the two preceding bodhis.
That which attains the fruit of universal knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) refers to the *vinaya* [of discipline] consisting in the abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion.
The meaning of the permanent subduing of greed and so forth;

furthermore, regarding the fruits of the śramaṇa that consist in the permanent abandonment of greed and so forth, these are the virtue of cessation through analytical discernment (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Regarding the shared and unshared mundane and supramundane virtues of the śrāvakas and the Tathāgata:

within the path-truth of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-mārga-satya*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are called "shared," while the ten powers (*daśabala*) and so forth are called "unshared."
"One who realizes this" refers to one who,
within these very dharmas of the realization of cessation and the path,
has personally realized the various knowledges of liberation.
To reveal it to others and cause them to realize it is called "realization.
This is understood within the context of the four meanings.
Jingyun: Regarding the meaning of "one-pointed grasping and reception," it refers to knowing that one's own mind grasps and takes up objects within the sensory sphere.
As stated below, regarding the second meaning of "experiencing" (*anubhava*):
it refers to knowing the sense of experiencing those three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
Regarding the third point, the meaning of "cognition as discernment":
this means that cognition has the sense of discerning and distinguishing. Tai says:
These are the objects of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
which serve as their respective four meanings.
Among these, three meanings are to be understood.
First, the meaning of the words refers to the teaching;
second, the meaning of the meaning refers to that which is explained,
which consists of ten types.
The one true characteristic is the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena;
the subsequent four are the four noble truths.
Sixth, regarding the characteristics of the distinctions among the categories of those very realities and so forth:
each of the five preceding meanings possesses its own distinct categories and subdivisions.
Seventh, regarding the characteristic of the relationship between the supported and the supporter:
The meaning is the supported (āśrita) and the name is the supporter (āśraya); this is the characteristic of their mutual connection.
Eighth, regarding the characteristics of the factors that obstruct thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) and so forth:
these are the afflictions (*kleśa*) underlying the four noble truths.
Ninth, "the characteristics of those factors conducive to them" refers to the characteristics of those various practices that are conducive to the underlying afflictions of the four truths.
Tenth, "the virtues of non-thorough knowledge and so forth, as well as thorough knowledge and so forth."
The meaning of the "three realms" refers to five kinds of realms:
first, the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*),
which is the place where [beings] dwell.
The second is the realm of sentient beings,
which refers to those who abide [in the teaching];
the dharma-realm is the dharma-gate that is taught.
That is to say, the aggregates, elements,
and bases; and the four realms of discipline,
which are the cessation truth of nirvana.
The fifth, the realm of the means for subduing,
is the Truth of the Path;
furthermore, the realm of subduing is the Noble Path.
The realm of skillful means for subduing is the preparatory stage prior to the path of seeing;
it is explained subsequently based on this.
Nirvāṇa is subsumed within the entry into the dharma-realm.
Thirteenth, the Gate of the Three Wisdoms.
The *Zhongjing* (Middle Scripture) says:
"The wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) involves inferential reasoning based on the textual words."
However, as it has been stated,
one has not yet mastered the underlying intent of the text,
nor has one attained direct realization.
This is not direct perception (pratyakṣa),
but rather inference (anumāna);
it merely remotely accords with nirvāṇa and liberation.
The wisdom consisting of reflection, which has not yet directly experienced the benefits of liberation,
likewise relies upon the literal expression.
It is not merely as it has been stated;
furthermore, its underlying intention has not yet been directly realized.
It excels the previously mentioned wisdom derived from hearing;
thus it is called "transformative and compliant. Although it excels the wisdom derived from hearing, [it is still surpassed by the wisdom of cultivation].
Nor has one yet directly experienced the benefit of liberation.
The wisdom consisting in cultivation likewise relies both on the literal expression and does not rely on the literal expression.
It is both as it is described and not as it is described.
Based on the wisdom of cultivation involving outflows (*sāsrava-bhāvanā-prajñā*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*),
images of both principles (*tattva*) and phenomena (*vastu*) arise and manifest before one.
Therefore, it is said that the mental image, which is the object of meditative concentration (samādhi) and shares the same nature as the knowable phenomena of the intended meaning,
is superior among the three types of wisdom and is called "extremely conducive to liberation."
Furthermore, one is able to receive and comprehend the meaning and benefit of liberation;
this differs from the Abhidharma,
where the wisdom derived from hearing relies solely upon the teachings.
Wisdom born of reflection may rely on the teachings or be independent of them;
wisdom born of cultivation is invariably independent of the teachings.
This is like three people learning to swim.
First, those near the shore;
second, those either near or away from it;
third, those entirely away from the shore.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* refutes this, saying:
"If reflection relies upon the teaching, it is not different from the wisdom of hearing;
if reflection is divorced from the teaching, it is not different from the wisdom of cultivation."
It should be said that the wisdom of hearing relies upon the teachings but cannot engage in reflection,
whereas the wisdom of reflection relies upon the teachings and is able to perform discernment. Bei says:
In this present text, the three types of wisdom are able to take the teaching as their object;
however, the wisdom of cultivation takes its arising as its object,
based on what is remote rather than what is proximate.
The fourteenth is the section on the distinction between knowledge (*jñāna*) and vision (*darśana*).
Sublime wisdom that takes the general dharma of principle as its object is called knowledge;
sublime wisdom that takes the specific dharmas of phenomena as its object is called vision.
Because one investigates according to the specific phenomena, one attains the vision of names.
This is the fifteenth gate, the Gate of Dispelling Characteristics and Abandoning Attachment.
Within it, there are three parts.
First, it clarifies that mental attention eliminates signs;
next, it clarifies that suchness is signless;
therefore, there is nothing to be discarded.
The subsequent section explains the scriptural passage.
First, it asks:
"By what mental attention (*manasikāra*) does a bodhisattva practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* proceed?"
This is the first question:
by means of what mental attention (*manasikāra*) does one cultivate calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*)?
As for the phrase "what [kind]":
This is the second question.
Regarding these two questions: what are the phenomena that are to be eliminated, and how are they eliminated?
The third question:
What kind of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) is able to dispel [the obstacles]?
The answer follows below.
The answer to the first question is: by means of mental attention directed toward suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding the statement that one cultivates calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) through mental attention directed toward suchness, it is said that one thereby eliminates the signs of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*) and the signs of their referents (*artha-nimitta*).
Regarding the second question, "What is it that is eliminated?
the answer is as follows: when one cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā by taking suchness as the object, the signs of phenomena (dharma-nimitta) and the signs of meaning (artha-nimitta) are eliminated;
that is, the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) is eliminated.
This passage explains that at the time of correct realization, the unchanging image appears as the semblance of *tathatā* (suchness).
As for the statement beginning with "If, regarding its name, etc.," it answers the third question: how does one eliminate all signs through meditative practice?
Now, the answer is given:
first, prior to the stages of the grounds (bhūmi),
one investigates according to reality through various modes of analytical inquiry.
Names and so forth are merely conventional designations.
Now, when entering the path of seeing and realizing suchness,
object and wisdom are equal, and there is no activity of conceptual discrimination.
It cannot be called "nature," nor can it be called the "basis.
Within the framework of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), it is said that [the object] depends upon consciousness, and consciousness is the basis.
Therefore, it is said: when one finds nothing to be apprehended in either the name or the intrinsic nature of the name, one likewise eliminates the characteristics of its basis.
Regarding the statement "as with names,

so it is up to [phrases]," this refers to the knowledge of phenomena through the aforementioned five types of knowledge— namely, knowledge of names, phrases, and phonemes— as well as the ten types of knowledge regarding meaning.
Therefore, one should know that the present analogy applies equally to names, phrases, syllables, and all meanings.
As for the statement "up to the elements" and "thus dispelling," it means the following:
In the preceding passage, one first knows phenomena through five modes of cognition,
knows meanings through ten modes of cognition,
and further knows five types of meaning.
Furthermore, one knows four meanings;
furthermore, one knows three meanings.
As for the three meanings:
First is the meaning of the text; second is the meaning of the meaning; third is the meaning of the realm (*dhātu*).
The meaning of the realm refers to the five realms, such as the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) and so forth.
When Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) perform this contemplation of the five kinds of realms, it is likewise nothing but consciousness, for consciousness serves as the basis.

Therefore it is said: "When one does not apprehend even the elements (*dhātu*) and the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the elements, one likewise does not observe the characteristics of their basis; in this way they are eliminated.
Next, it is explained that because suchness is realized as being without signs (*animitta*), there is nothing to be eliminated.

Question: When non-conceptual wisdom directly realizes suchness, can the characteristics of that suchness be eliminated? Answer: [The answer is: No. Why? Because suchness is the very nature of all phenomena; it is not something that can be removed. Furthermore, since non-conceptual wisdom has suchness as its object, there is no other suchness apart from that which is realized by this wisdom. Therefore, it cannot be eliminated. Moreover, because suchness is the ultimate reality, it is unconditioned and eternally abiding; thus, it is impossible for it to be eliminated. Finally, because suchness is the true nature of all phenomena, it is not distinct from them. Since all phenomena cannot be eliminated, how could their true nature be eliminated? For these reasons, the characteristics of suchness cannot be eliminated. However, the adventitious defilements—such as the grasping at signs and conceptualizations—which obscure suchness, can indeed be eliminated through the power of non-conceptual wisdom. It is only these adventitious stains that are to be abandoned, not the suchness itself. Thus, while the obscurations are removed, the true nature remains as it is. This is the meaning.
If, at the time of direct realization, one perceives any semblance of characteristics or anything to be apprehended,
there is something to be discarded;
however, within the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness) thus understood, there are no characteristics whatsoever and nothing to be apprehended.
What, then, could be dispatched?
This text explains that realized wisdom (pramāṇa-jñāna) possesses no objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga).
Since the objective aspect is absent, the subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga) is likewise non-existent.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
seeing that which is signless, one says, "I have explained and fully understood this; it is not something that others are capable of comprehending or subduing."
Before realization, one grasps the characteristics of the meaning of phenomena;
at the very moment of realizing suchness, [one realizes it].
The characteristics of the dharmas and meanings previously subdued are not yet fully realized and penetrated at this time of correct realization; furthermore,
there are other characteristics that must be subdued by further means.
Therefore, it is said that this thorough comprehension cannot be suppressed by anything else.
The following explains the passage from the sutra:
"World-Honored One, what is this so-called 'mind capable of observation'?"
The question, "Regarding the essence that is able to contemplate,
based on which suchness is this statement made? asks about the suchness that is the object of contemplation.
The answer below:
The three types of wisdom are that which are capable of observation.
It is in reliance upon the thoroughly distinguished suchness (*pariniṣpanna-tathatā*) that this statement was made.
Since it is stated in the analogy that clear water, a clean mirror, and an undisturbed spring pool are capable of reflecting the image of a face,

one knows that when, in the application [of the teaching], the mind is well-cultivated such that it is capable of perceiving True Suchness (tathatā), this is known as the discernment of True Suchness through the perspective of Consciousness-Only (vijñaptimātra).
By means of the gateway of *vijñapti-mātra*, all objective spheres are shadows of the mind.
First, one contemplates that objects are *vijñapti-mātra*; subsequently, one contemplates that consciousness is like [an illusion].
It is called "the suchness of discernment" (*vijñapti-tathatā*); therefore, it is said that this is taught based on the suchness of discernment.
The sixteenth is the section on dispelling characteristics by relying on emptiness.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the ten aspects of the contemplation on emptiness for the purpose of elimination;
second, the discernment of the general characteristics of emptiness.
The preceding section has three parts.
First, it clarifies how the seventeen emptinesses eliminate the ten signs.
Second, it clarifies the fruits obtained through emptiness.
The latter part clarifies the principle of removing signs through the contemplation of emptiness.
Regarding this, first there is a question and subsequently an answer.
Within the question, how many kinds of signs are difficult to eliminate?
This is the first question.
"Who is able to dispel it?
is the second question.
"Good son, there are ten characteristics.
This answers the first question:
emptiness is able to eliminate them.
Answering the second question:
One must know that the ten signs are all thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) and are all eliminated through the contemplation of emptiness.
First, regarding the adherence to the meaning of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being definitively existent:
one eliminates this by contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*),
because the objects of such adherence encompass all phenomena.
One contemplates all phenomena as empty and eliminates them.
Second, the four truths, beginning with suffering, are all established;
because the truth of suffering comes first, it is designated as "establishment."
In this context, the manner in which suffering is established through grasping is presented.
This involves two types of clinging:
first, the clinging that suffering possesses the nature of arising, ceasing, abiding, and changing.
This is the contemplation that eliminates the mark of emptiness;
it removes the two types of grasping at suffering and the continuous succession [of existence].
The contemplation of the emptiness of no prior or posterior can correctly eliminate this.
That which is conceptually constructed is fundamentally non-existent; therefore, there is no sequence of prior or subsequent stages in its elimination.
Third, it is by means of understanding that the six sense faculties are the apprehenders [of objects].
There is then attachment and clinging toward the internal body;
this is eliminated by contemplating internal emptiness.
Because of the grasping at a self, the conceit "I am" arises.
When one contemplates emptiness as being without anything to be apprehended,
the self cannot be found;
how, then, could pride arise?
The fourth [point] can be understood according to the text.
The sixth is the grasping at the mark of internal bliss;
this is dispelled by internal emptiness.
The attachment to external objects as pure is dispelled by the emptiness of the external;
the attachment to the presence of men and women, their service, and the suitability of requisites [is dispelled by the emptiness of the internal].
It is eliminated by means of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*); furthermore, it may also be universally eliminated through the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*),
which dispels attachments such as internal bliss and external purity.
Sixth, when one understands that sentient beings are established within the external vessel-world,
one may then cling to the existence of infinite characteristics in the ten directions;
this is dispelled by the great emptiness.
Seventh, they take those four emptinesses to be liberation,
yet they dispel them with the emptiness of the conditioned.
Eighth, if they cling to the characteristics of the two kinds of selflessness.
It is removed by ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
If one clings to the characteristic of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra-lakṣaṇa*), it is treated by the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).
If one clings to the dependent nature as being the characteristic of the ultimate,
it is treated by the emptiness of the cause of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
if one clings to the perfected nature as being distinct from the ultimate, [it is treated by the emptiness of the non-existence of other-nature].
This is remedied by the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
"Grasping" is as stated in the text.
Tenth is the grasping that there exists a reality of the nine aforementioned remedies, namely emptiness.
One immediately contemplates "emptiness of emptiness" as the remedy;
that is, one contemplates that even the emptiness which is capable of removing [afflictions] is itself empty.
Next, the fruit obtained through emptiness is explained.
The meaning of the question:
When the ten types of thoroughly imagined characteristics mentioned above are eliminated,
what further [characteristics] are eliminated?
Furthermore, from what signs does one attain liberation?
The answer is:
when one contemplates emptiness and eliminates the ten types of signs that are conceptually imputed (*parikalpita*).
Within the mind of the contemplation of emptiness, there still remains the dependent nature appearing as an image of emptiness that manifests in accordance with the empty mind.
From this contemplation of emptiness, one enters into realized wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*),
whereby the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the image of emptiness is eliminated.
Once the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) has been eliminated, one is liberated from the seeds of all bonds of defiled appearances;
even the grasping at a mind that is liberated is entirely abandoned.
Therefore, it is said that they are also eliminated.
The following clarifies the principle by which the contemplation of emptiness eliminates these signs;
each individual contemplation of emptiness eliminates ten signs.
As for the statement that "the first emptiness remedies the first characteristic" and so forth,
this is spoken in terms of predominance;
it is a teaching of direct antidotes corresponding [to those characteristics].
It is not that one does not individually contemplate and treat all characteristics;
this can be understood through analogies.
From here on, the general characteristic of emptiness is explained.
First the question is posed and then the answer is given. Within the answer, first there is praise for the question and permission to speak,
followed by the actual response to the question.

It is said: When one is about to become deluded regarding the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) and the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), one gives rise to the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
If one awakens to the fact that the dependent and the perfected natures are not the objects grasped by that imagination, [one realizes them as they truly are].
To know that which is grasped as empty is called "universal emptiness" (*sāmānya-śūnyatā*). Tai says:
When distinguished individually,
there are seventeen kinds of emptiness;
when summarized collectively, [there is one].

It is only within the characteristics of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) that one is ultimately and completely free from the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
and that this [imagined nature] is entirely non-apprehendable;
thus, all emptiness is fully encompassed within the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Therefore, it is called "universal emptiness.
Once this emptiness is realized, there are two benefits:
first, one does not lose correct practice.
Second, it is free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Seventeenth, it may be understood through several categories of inclusion.
The eighteenth is the gateway of cause and effect.
Regarding the śamatha and vipaśyanā of the stage of training,
pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the correct view derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*) serve as its causes.
This is the contributory cause (pratyaya-hetu).
If the seeds of śamatha and vipaśyanā serve as the primary cause (hetu-hetu).
As for the fruit of śamatha and vipaśyanā,
it consists precisely of the perfectly pure mind and wisdom of the Buddha-stage.
Furthermore, it includes all supramundane wholesome dharmas possessed by arhats and Buddhas.
All of these are the fruits of training in śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The nineteenth is the gateway of activity,
which refers to the ability to liberate oneself from the bondage of signs and the bondage of coarse heaviness (dausthulya).
The bond of grossness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*) refers to the seeds of the cognitive aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the various afflictions;
the bond of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) refers precisely to the seeds of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the afflictions.
Furthermore, the manifestation of the characteristics of subject and object is also a twofold bondage.
This concludes the twentieth gate: the obstacles to śamatha and vipaśyanā.
First, the five fetters are distinguished;
subsequently, the five hindrances are distinguished.
Within the former, there is attachment to the body.
Coveting wealth is an obstacle to cessation;
it prevents one from attaining mastery over the noble Dharma.
The obstacles to the contemplation of the fruit are:
delighting in living in company,
and having few desires and being easily contented.
Not delighting in extensive cultivation obstructs both śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Regarding the inability to engage in cultivation due to the first [reason]:
One delights in living in company.
Because of the second [hindrance], one who has not reached the culmination of the practice undertaken fails to achieve small desire and contentment.
The obstructions are as stated in the text.
The twenty-second is the gate of perfect purity.
Previously, the obstruction of lethargy and drowsiness regarding contemplation was analyzed.
Now, as for the statement that "the path of the mind is fulfilled by dispelling lethargy and drowsiness," it is because calm abiding gives rise to insight;
calm abiding is the cause and insight is the result.
By citing the removal of obstacles to the fruit, the perfection of the cause is revealed.
Even the thorough elimination of all agitation (*auddhatya*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*) is called the fulfillment of the path of insight (*vipaśyanā-mārga*);
this likewise cites the removal of obstacles to the cause to reveal the fulfillment of the path of the fruit (*phala-mārga*).
The twenty-third section: The Gate of Distraction.
When calm abiding and insight are manifest, there are five mental factors that cause distraction.
First is mental distraction,
which refers to bodhisattvas abandoning the Mahāyāna and instead engaging in the mental orientations of the two vehicles.
Second is external distraction (*bahirdhā-vikṣepa*).
Regarding the discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) associated with the five external sensual desires, it takes the discursive thoughts as its essence;
and regarding the external objects, it takes the distracted mental faculty (*citta-rāja*) that allows the mind to flow and disperse outwardly.
Third is internal mental distraction,
which refers to a person who has already abandoned desire [but] gives rise to attachment toward meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and so forth due to lethargy (*styāna*) and other such factors.
This is called internal distraction.
Fourth is distraction regarding signs,
which refers to the images that appear within internal meditative concentration.

To attend to and conceptualize the internal meditative concentration while grasping at the external signs of perceived objects is called "distraction by signs" (*nimitta-vikṣepa*) and "distraction by the five heavy burdens" (*dauṣṭhulya-vikṣepa*).
This refers to reckoning the joy and bliss within meditative concentration as "mine," and giving rise to pride by reckoning the coarse and heavy body as "self";
this is called the distraction of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).
The twenty-third section: The Gate of Overcoming Obstructions.

Regarding the removal of the defilements of afflictions, karma, and birth pertaining to the evil destinies in the first stage (*bhūmi*), the following seventy-eight [verses] distinguish twenty-three types of delusion (*moha*).
First, the attachment to dharmas;
second, the defilement of the miserable destinies,
which comprises afflictions, karma, and birth.
In this context, there is only the second [obstruction]. The *Dilun* states:
"The obstacle of the ordinary person's mark of self (*ātman*)."
However, the first stage is as previously stated;
the second stage remedies the obstacle of the active manifestation of subtle erroneous attachments.
Below, it is explained that the second stage has two types of delusion.
First, the delusion of subtle erroneous clinging;
second, the delusion regarding the various courses of karma.
This refers to the delusion concerning the distinctions between the three types of karma and the three types of conduct.
Among these, there is only the first one.
The *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) states:
"Improper conduct constitutes an obstacle to the various bodies and so forth of the assembly."
This corresponds to the second [stage];
the third stage overcomes the obstacle of sensual desire.
As will be explained below, there are two types of delusion in these three stages.
First, sensual desire obstructs meditative concentration;
second, delusion regarding the perfection of the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining.
In this case, only the former exists.
The *Dilun* says:
"The characteristic of darkness corresponds to sensual desire."
The obstacle of forgetting the dharmas such as hearing, reflection,
and cultivation corresponds to the second [ground].
The obstacle of attachment to meditative concentration and attachment to the Dharma, which is remedied on the fourth ground, is as follows:
Because there is attachment to the Dharma— such as when one seeks the Dharma by throwing oneself into a fire pit on the third bhūmi—
it is said that there are two types of such attachment to the Dharma, which will be explained below.
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states that the fourth stage has two delusions:
first, attachment to meditative concentration;
second, attachment to the Dharma.
The *Dilun* states: "Regarding the obstacles of pride concerning the understanding of dharmas,
they are collectively not two."
Because craving and pride are distinct;
furthermore, pride may arise from attaining superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and understanding the Dharma.
Pride arises from [attaining] meditative concentration, which is the practice of the Dharma, and from upholding the teaching of the Dharma.
Collectively, these are called the obstacles of pride regarding the dharmas of liberation.
On the fifth stage, one remedies the obstacle of being unilaterally oriented toward either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa;
this is the same as the [remedies for] the two lower stages.
In this context, these are combined as one;
below, they are divided into two: "turning away" and "tending toward.
The *Dilun* says:
The pride of physical purity is an obstacle;
because one gives rise to pride by maintaining the body through the purification of the mental path-factors (*cittamārgāṅga*),
one turns one's back on saṃsāra and heads toward nirvāṇa.
This is largely the same as that.
On the sixth stage, one remedies the obstacle of the frequent manifestation of signs;
on the fifth stage, one abandons the two delusions of aversion and pursuit.
Now, in the sixth stage, one eliminates the mind that is largely weary and averse [to practice].
Because the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination manifest frequently,
one eliminates the obstacle of the frequent manifestation of such characteristics.
The text below states that there are two delusions in the sixth stage.
Regarding "the delusion of observing the flow of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they manifest":
this refers to the delusion of being unable to realize dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in the fifth stage.
In the second stage, delusion regarding the frequent manifestation of the two signs is predominant;
although the tendency toward aversion and attraction has been severed in the fifth stage,
the mind characterized by aversion and attraction still frequently manifests.
Regarding this, it corresponds to the second stage.
The *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) states:
"The subtle habitual tendencies of afflictions constitute an obstruction."
In total, there are two types.
That which precedes the [gross] form is called "subtle.
Regarding the seventh stage, it counteracts the subtle manifestation of the obstacles to the signs of phenomena.
That which is abandoned at the seventh stage, wherein one still perceives subtle arising and ceasing,
is called the "obstruction of the manifestation of subtle signs.
The lower treatise states that there are two types of ignorance at the seventh stage.
First, the manifestation of subtle characteristics;
this refers to what is being discussed here.
Second, the delusion of exerting effort toward the signless.
Although there is still effort regarding the signless in the seventh stage,
one enters true contemplation for a long duration;
thus, the sixth stage cannot obstruct the seventh stage.
Therefore, in the seventh stage, one abandons the delusion of exerting effort regarding the signless (*animitta*).
The *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) says:
"The subtle habitual obstruction of signs."
This should also be considered the first [instance].
The eighth stage overcomes the obstacle of effortful engagement with the signless (*animitta*) and the lack of mastery over signs (*nimitta*).
As it says below: "The eighth stage has two types of delusion."
In the eighth stage, there is non-conceptuality and effortlessness;
within conventional appearances, there is effort for the benefit of others but no effort for one's own benefit.
The obstacles of the seventh stage differ from those of the eighth stage.
In the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), there is the abandonment of one [type of ignorance]: first, the exertion regarding the signless (*animitta*);
second, the delusion regarding mastery over signs (*nimitta-vaśitā-moha*).
These are distinguished from those [abandoned] herein by way of being either opened out or subsumed.
The *Dilun* states:
"Regarding the presence of obstacles to practice within the signless,
there is only the first [obstacle]."
The ninth stage overcomes the obstacle of lacking mastery over skillful speech in all its aspects.
As it says below: "In the ninth stage there are two forms of delusion:
first, the delusion regarding the lack of mastery over the dhāraṇīs of subsequent wisdom and eloquence concerning immeasurable teachings and immeasurable phrases and syllables."
Second is the delusion regarding mastery over eloquence (*pratibhāna-vaśitā-moha*).
This differs from the former in terms of its analytical and synthetic treatment.
The *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) states:
The obstacle of being unable to properly benefit sentient beings;
the obstacle of not attaining the realization of the perfect Dharma-body, which is remedied by the tenth stage.
As the lower treatise states:
The tenth stage has two types of ignorance:
first, ignorance regarding the great supernormal powers;
second, ignorance regarding the realization of subtle secrets.
The opening and closing of these categories differ between that [text] and this one.
The *Dilun* states:
"The tenth is the obstacle of not attaining mastery over all phenomena."
It is the same in this regard as well.

Concerning the Tathāgata stage, that which serves as the antidote to the subtle and most extremely subtle afflictive obstructions and cognitive obstructions is the dharma for abandoning these two obstructions through the lowest-of-the-low grade of the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" level.
If one wishes to know [the distinction between them], attachment is the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), while obstruction is the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This text provides clear scriptural proof.
Regarding the phrase, "Because one can permanently destroy such hindrances, one ultimately realizes unattached and unimpeded omniscience and all-seeing wisdom," the subsequent treatise states:
"In the stage of the Tathāgata, there are two types of ignorance."
First, there is the extremely subtle attachment to all objects of knowledge,
which is also the affliction of non-perception in its lowest degree;
second, there is the extremely subtle obscuration of ignorance.
It is also of the inferior grade known by non-perception; therefore,
it is the same as that [state],
differing only in its expansion and contraction.
Although the *Dilun* does not explicitly mention an eleventh hindrance,
the tenth hindrance— the hindrance to attaining mastery over all phenomena—
encompasses both the Buddha’s subtle attachments and subtle obstructions.
Regarding the tenth obstacle, it is explained figuratively that it obstructs the Buddha because it is the most subtle;
in reality, however, it is severed by the vajra-mind.
Regarding this meaning, there are two interpretations.
One interpretation states that, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, one enters the first stage upon severing the obstacles of the first stage;
the remaining stages follow this same principle.
Furthermore, as the *Benyeyejing* (Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra) states:
Beyond the tenth stage, there is the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi-bhūmi*).
One studies this for thirteen thousand kalpas;
having thus abided in the stage of Equal Enlightenment and severed the obstacles of the Buddha-stage, one first enters the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-abhisambodhi*).
First, it is said that based on this passage concerning the eleven obstacles and so forth, it is taught that wisdom also abandons its own respective obstacles.
Second, regarding the twenty-fourth gate of cultivating and realizing bodhi, it says:
"If various bodhisattvas have already attained śamatha and vipaśyanā, relying upon the seven kinds of true thusness, up to internal correct reflection, and so forth."
In the stage of preparatory application prior to the [first] bhūmi,
one contemplates the seven kinds of true thusness according to their designations;
having thoroughly examined and thoroughly reflected upon them, one establishes the seven kinds of true thusness.
By means of correct internal reflection upon the nature of things,
through such reflection,
one is able to relinquish all subtle signs.
This means that as the various mental images—
the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*)— cease, one simultaneously abandons all the characteristics that follow the mind.
Tai [Zongyi] said:
Among these, the seven suchnesses are not the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
The former masters, relying on the *Madhyāntavibhāga*,
state that although all seven kinds of suchness are suchness,
they specifically speak of "the suchness of the truth of suffering."
The Truth of Suffering is named according to its designator.
That which is said to be "the mental factors of grasping, experiencing, and discerning the characteristics of defilement and purity" refers precisely to the four foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding the characteristics of suffering that involve change and those that do not:

the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) are termed "possessing change," while the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is termed "without change."
Furthermore, it is explained that transformation is the characteristic of suffering;
that which is without transformation is not suffering,
for it lacks substantial reality.
Regarding the distinct characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*): they are distinct because form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth, differ from one another.
Regarding their common characteristics (*sālakṣaṇa*): they are common because they share such qualities as suffering (*duḥkha*) and impermanence (*anityatā*).
Alternatively, having known that all things are all things, one possesses the characteristic of all things.
Since one knows that all phenomena are already all things, they possess the characteristic of all things.
Because he dwells extensively in such practice, [he attains this].
Having well cultivated and purified the mind,
when the seven distinct types of individually realized penetrating knowledge arise regarding the seven suchnesses, this is called the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). This is because,
by means of the individual realization of each of the seven suchnesses as a skillful means, [the path of seeing is established].
Therefore, one subsequently enters the contemplation of perception;
when the wisdom that penetrates all such [realities] arises through this contemplation, it is called the Path of Vision (darśanamārga),
which is precisely the entry into the First Stage (bhūmi).
Because of attaining this, one is said to have entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
This refers to the stage of entry;
as for "being born into the family of the Tathāgata," it means:
This explains the fault of being a householder;
furthermore, being able to enjoy the superior virtues of this stage constitutes the other six faults.

Because he has previously attained calm abiding and insight, he has already attained two kinds of objects of focus: namely, the object of focus that is a conceptual image and the object of focus that is a non-conceptual image.
This text itself judges that the two kinds of images are the objects of focus for the śamatha and vipaśyanā prior to that stage;
since one attains the path of seeing at this present time, one further realizes the object of focus known as the "limit of phenomena" (vastuparyantatā).
This characteristic clearly explains the third object of focus for cultivation and realization.
For now, we shall speak of the object of focus for the path of seeing;
that is, true suchness (tathatā) is designated as the "limit of phenomena" (vastuparyanta).
Because that suchness pervades all dharmas of the truths, it is called the "limit of the truths" (*satyakoṭi*).
This passage explains that the wisdom of realization takes suchness as its object without transformation into an image;
yet, if it were to transform into an image resembling that suchness, [it would not be so].
This is precisely what is subsumed under non-conceptual images.
Why, then, is it determined that the objects of these two types of images belong to the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*)?
Furthermore, why is the object of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) designated solely as the "limit of phenomena" (*vastuparyantatā*)?
Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of the path of meditation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in each successive stage, wherein one directs the mind toward these three types of objects of focus (*ālambana*),
this clarifies that the knowledge of the path of meditation takes the limits of phenomena (*vastuparyantatā*) as its object.
Because subsequent knowledge takes two kinds of images as its objects,
it is said that one attends to and contemplates these three objects during the path of cultivation.
The following provides an analogy.
By means of a fine wedge one extracts a coarse wedge;
by means of the superior path one abandons the inferior path,
gradually eliminating both signs (*nimitta*) and coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Up until the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
this is called the realization of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, regarding the object of focus for the fulfillment of what is to be done:
It is then determined that this object belongs to the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).
Because it is the cognitive domain in which all activities of the Buddha-ground are completely fulfilled,
it is called the "object-condition of the fulfillment of what was to be done" (*kṛtaniṣṭhā-ālambana*).
What is the object of focus?
It does not depart from the previous three:
it is the ultimate limit of the truths, which serves as the object for the śamatha and vipaśyanā realized by the Tathāgata regarding the principle.
The śamatha and vipaśyanā associated with the truths as objects of the Tathāgata are the two images;
these three serve as the objects of the Tathāgata’s śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Collectively, they are termed the "object of the fulfillment of what is to be accomplished."
The twenty-fifth is the gateway of eliciting majestic power.
When a bodhisattva skillfully understands the six sense bases,
they are able to elicit vast majestic power.
First, "skillfully knowing the arising of the mind" refers to knowing,
as it truly is, the distinctions in the arising of the sixteen types of outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) minds. First, that which cannot be cognized.
The mode of activity of the ālayavijñāna is difficult to discern;
because it abides firmly and continues uninterruptedly,
it is called "firmly abiding."
That which possesses the capacity for the continuous arising of the receptacle-world and its contents, and which is capable of transformation and cognition,
is called the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
This is called "grasping and maintaining.
It grasps and maintains the seeds of the sense faculties (*indriya*), the great elements (*mahābhūta*), and all phenomena.

Second, regarding the arising of consciousness that takes various modes of appearance as its objects—namely, the conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that simultaneously apprehends all objects such as forms and so forth.
This refers to the sixth consciousness, which, in accordance with its various modes of cognitive engagement (*vikalpa*),
suddenly grasps all phenomena; therefore,
it is said to have "various modes of activity" (*nānā-ākāra*).
Regarding the simultaneous apprehension of form and so forth, as well as the simultaneous apprehension of internal and external objects and their corresponding sensations:
it is one's own consciousness that simultaneously apprehends the internal and external objects of contact and thereby gives rise to sensation.

Alternatively, it refers to the discriminative mental consciousness that, in a single instant, enters into multiple meditative absorptions, perceives multiple Buddha-lands, and beholds multiple Tathāgatas.
This refers to the subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of bodhisattvas on the great stages, who perceive many Buddhas while in meditative concentration;
because it is not direct realized wisdom (*sākṣāt-kriyā-jñāna*), it is termed "conceptual.

Regarding the statement that consciousness arises with the objects of the small and great characteristics of the third and fourth [dhyānas], this refers to consciousness bound to the realms of desire and form.
Because they take as their objects the bodies within two realms,
they are categorized as small or great;
the next three minds take the four formless [realms] as their objects.
Eighth, regarding the arising of the signless consciousness (*animitta-vijñāna*), which refers to supramundane consciousness:
this means that untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) is devoid of the seven kinds of signs,
and is thus called "signless consciousness," as well as the consciousness that takes cessation (*nirodha*) as its object.
The consciousness that takes the signless object as its sphere, whether it be a mind associated with outflows or free from outflows,
is called signless consciousness.
Furthermore, it refers to the consciousness that understands and takes the cessation-attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*) as its object.
Some versions read the character "jian" (減, to diminish) instead;
this must be a scribal error.
Next, there are five minds that correspond to consciousness functioning in conjunction with the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
Following these, there are three minds that clarify defiled, pure, and neutral consciousness.
The remainder of the text is easily understood.
The twenty-sixth section, the Gate of Receiving Nirvana:
As stated in the text, within the state of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), two types of sensation (*vedanā*) are eternally extinguished.
The first is the sensation of the heavy impediments (*dausthulya*) of the basis.
The six internal sense faculties that give rise to sensation are called the "basis.
Their substance is contaminated (*sāsrava*).
They are termed "dysfunctional" (*dausthulya*) because they are pursued by the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of afflictions and an unpliant nature.
First is the sensation of the heaviness (dausthulya) that serves as the basis for names; second is the sensation of the objects which are their results,
meaning that the five external coarse [objects] are produced by the power of the five internal faculties and are thus the results of those internal faculties.
Therefore, it is called "feeling with that as its object.
Because it arises in dependence upon that [object], it is called "feeling with the fruit of that as its object.
According to this principle, the essential natures of these two types of feeling are not necessarily distinct.
However, the two types of sensation are distinguished based on the faculties and their objects.
Within the sensations of the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) that serve as their basis, there are four kinds.
The first is the material basis (*rūpy-āśraya*).
That is, the five consciousnesses experience it;
the two formless [realms] have the mind as their support,
that is, the mental consciousness experiences it.
These are the two types of sensation pertaining to body and mind.
Third is the sensation of the grossness (*dausthulya*) of the fully perfected fruit,
which refers to present sensation.
Fourth is the experience of results that have not yet reached fulfillment,
which refers to the experience of future causes;
that is to say, karma and afflictions are the causes for future experience.
This is called the feeling of the cause.
There are also four kinds of feelings regarding the objective realm that is its fruit:
first, the feeling of support.
That is to say, the receptacle world is the supporting dharma;
the sensation produced by taking it as an object is called "supporting sensation.
Second, the sensation of requisites may be understood in the same way.
Third is the experience of enjoyment (*paribhoga-vedanā*).
That is, the two types of sensation experience the receptacle world and its material requisites;
this is called the experience of enjoyment.
The four types of clinging to sensation:
clinging to sensation regarding material wealth,
and [clinging to sensation] regarding the extent of the cessation of sensation within the realms of *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* nirvāṇa.
Jingyun says:
Within the realm of *nirvāṇa-with-remainder*, although the fruit has not yet reached full completion, all that was to be experienced has already been extinguished;
at the moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*), the substance of karma and afflictions has already been completely severed.
Only then can one possess the remainder:
that is, experiencing the feeling born of contact through clear knowledge (*vidyā-sparśaja-vedanā*), which is the antidote to that [craving],
and which is associated with the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*).
This refers to the feeling born of contact with clear [consciousness]. Regarding "shared experience":
it refers to the experience of the shared vessel-world.
This refers specifically to the sensation of maintenance and sustenance; for brevity, the sensation of utilizing requisites and resources is not mentioned,
with the sole exception of the sensation of attachment.
Because it is associated with greed;
or alternatively, because for one who experiences the fruition that has already been fully accomplished,
there exists within that fully accomplished experience both the presence of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and the absence of coarse heaviness.
Now, within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), there exists only sensation free from coarse heaviness (dausthulya);
hence the word "or" is used.
For brevity, it does not mention the sensation that takes the material basis as its support, nor the sensation that takes the immaterial basis as its support.
Because [the outflows] still arise even for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
the second text explains it thus:
furthermore, both kinds of sensation have all been extinguished.
This means that the retribution of the heavy burdens (dausthulya) of the basis and the experience of the objects that are their fruits have both been completely eliminated.
